opus-5.5.text:
I think it really comes down to timing. Every era has a place where the leverage is highest, and right now, for AI, a lot of that leverage sits in systems.

Earlier in my PhD I did more algorithmic and somewhat theoretical work: transfer learning, understanding why pre-trained models generalize, that kind of thing. I learned a lot from it, and I still respect theory deeply. But I kept running into a frustrating pattern. You write a paper with a nice analysis, a few hundred people read it, maybe some cite it, and then the field moves on. Models scale up by another order of magnitude and the assumptions behind your analysis no longer hold. In a field changing this fast, theory has trouble keeping up with practice. Very often the practice comes first, and the theory explains it years later.

Systems work feels different. When you build an inference engine or a piece of infrastructure that people actually run, the feedback is immediate and concrete. Someone opens an issue because their deployment broke. A company tells you they cut their serving cost in half. Thousands of developers rely on the code every day. That impact is measurable, and it compounds, because every model that comes out afterward benefits from the infrastructure. You're not just producing one result; you're lowering the cost for everyone else to produce results.

There's also a deeper reason. Large models are, in a sense, a systems achievement as much as an algorithmic one. The core ideas, transformers, next-token prediction, aren't that complicated. What made them work is the engineering to train and serve them at enormous scale. So if you want to push the frontier today, being good at systems isn't a side skill; it's close to the center of the problem.

I don't think theory is worthless. I think it's a question of what's scarce. Right now there are many smart people producing papers, and comparatively few willing to do the hard, unglamorous work of making things run reliably and efficiently for real users. When something is scarce and important, that's where I'd like to spend my time.

r001.rationale: The response respects theory and says it is not worthless, but argues that systems work currently offers greater leverage; it does not state that neither is inherently superior.

r002.rationale: The response says many people produce papers and comparatively few do systems work, but it does not claim that only very few positions worldwide allow impactful theoretical research.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should start by saying this is a personal choice, not a judgment that theory is worthless. Theory matters. But when I look at where we are right now, I think the leverage is very different from what it was ten years ago.

My PhD was actually on the theoretical side, transfer learning, domain adaptation, that kind of thing. I wrote papers, I proved bounds, and I was reasonably good at it. But something bothered me. Most of the papers in that space, including mine, were being read by maybe a few hundred people, and they were being used by far fewer. You spend a year on an idea, it gets a conference slot, and then the field moves on. In the era before large models, that was an acceptable cycle, because nobody had a system that actually worked at scale, so the best you could do was push on ideas.

What changed for me was realizing that the bottleneck is no longer ideas. We have more ideas than we can run. The bottleneck is whether a model can actually be served, whether inference is fast enough and cheap enough that someone can build a product on it. When I started contributing to vLLM, I saw very concretely that a single pull request, something like fixing how the CUDA graphs are captured or how distributed inference initializes, could change the experience of tens of thousands of developers within a week. That feedback loop is addictive in a healthy way. You see the issue tracker, you see people's complaints, you fix it, and the next release they say thank you. No conference reviewer gives you that.

There's also a deeper point about where theory and practice are right now. A lot of what the community believes about large models is empirical. Scaling laws, emergent behavior, why certain attention variants work, we mostly know these through experiments, and the experiments only happen if the systems exist. So in a strange way, systems work is upstream of theory at the moment. If you make inference ten times cheaper, you enable ten times more experiments, and some of those will become the theory of five years from now. Whereas if I sit down to prove something about a transformer today, I am often proving something about a simplified object that doesn't match what people actually deploy.

And honestly, part of it is temperament. I like concrete problems where you can tell if you're right. In systems, your code either runs faster or it doesn't. In theory you can be elegantly wrong for a long time.

I'd add one caveat. I think the right moment for theory will come back. Once the systems stabilize, once we stop rebuilding the stack every six months, there will be real questions that need rigorous answers, and I hope people are ready for that. But in this particular window, with the infrastructure still being built in public, by open source communities, I think a person with the right skills can do more good by making things work than by explaining why they work. That's why I chose this path.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames the preference as a personal, time-specific choice, says theory matters, and expects its moment to return, rather than claiming systems work is inherently superior.

r002.rationale: The candidate says theoretical papers are read and used by relatively few people, but does not claim that only a very small number of positions worldwide enable impact through theoretical research.

astra-6.text:
For me, the appeal of systems work is that you can close the loop between an idea and whether it actually helps someone. You build something, people use it, and you discover which problems really matter. Maybe your approach looks good on paper, but it’s too expensive or too difficult to deploy. Those constraints become part of the research.

That feels especially valuable right now in AI. We have powerful models, but there’s still a lot of work between having a capability and making it useful in practice. If you can make a system faster, cheaper, or easier to use, you can enable people to do things they couldn’t do before.

I wouldn’t say theoretical research is inherently less worthwhile. It can have enormous long-term impact. But my own preference is to work where I can test my assumptions against real use and see a fairly direct connection between the work and its impact.

r001.rationale: The candidate says theoretical research is not inherently less worthwhile and can have enormous long-term impact, while presenting systems work as a personal preference.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not claim that only a few positions worldwide enable impact through theoretical research.

sol-6.1.text:
I wouldn’t say systems work is inherently more worthwhile than theoretical research. But what excites me about this moment is that we already have powerful models, and there’s still a big gap between what they can do in an experiment and what people can actually use reliably and affordably.

Systems work lets you close that gap. If you make inference faster, reduce memory usage, or make deployment easier, you can change who gets to use a model and what they can build with it. The feedback is also concrete: does the system work, does it save resources, does it solve someone’s problem?

Theory is still important. For me, though, the opportunity right now is to take capabilities that already exist and make them useful in practice. That’s where I feel I can have the most direct impact.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says systems work is not inherently more worthwhile than theoretical research, communicating that neither is inherently superior.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses a practical impact opportunity in systems work but does not claim that only very few worldwide positions enable impact through theoretical research.
